s07.slug: MONDAY · 7:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: The fourth-floor lounge is empty at twenty to eight, the Zenith dark on its cart. Priya has struck back since Sunday. Taped to the frame of the whiteboard, at an angle that suggests a struggle, is a new laminate: THIS WHITEBOARD IS THE PROPERTY OF RESIDENTIAL LIFE. (IT IS NOT A NEWSPAPER.) Under it, in Margot’s capitals, the weekend has gone up anyway.

body: He reads it top to bottom for a line he could argue with and comes away empty-handed, which is Margot’s whole method.

The east stairwell smells of cold concrete and other people’s cigarettes. On the fourth-floor landing the window opens its six inches onto the Lagoon going navy, and if he holds the RAZR up into the top corner of the frame, it finds its bar. Lena’s call is at 8:04, two floors down, every night; he has twenty minutes of stairwell before it’s hers. On Glenwood Avenue it’s twenty to eleven.

Gina answers in a whisper, from under something. He can hear the covers. She whispers the way she texts, all lowercase, and she has clearly been crying earlier and is finished with that and would like that noted.

“it was religion,” she says. “mrs d is doing the corporal works of mercy. she put them on the board like a grocery list. feed the hungry. clothe the naked. visit the imprisoned. and ashley vrabel goes, oh, gina’s the class expert on that one.” A breath under the blanket. “and everybody laughed. even kelsey. kelsey laughed and then looked at me like *sorry* and then laughed again. and mrs d said *ladies*. just ladies. and kept going. we did bury the dead next.”

“Who’s Ashley Vrabel?” “nobody. she does color guard.” The whisper goes hot. “and her dad got a dui last christmas, it was all over st brigid’s, and SHE’S calling ME.” The capitals come through the whisper somehow. Jack has his free hand flat on the cold window frame.

Then, because she’s Gina, she changes the subject in the direction of worse. “dad turned it back on. low. like you said.” The garage arrives whole: the space heater ticking, the radio on the shelf over the Stroh’s fridge, his father in the folding chair with the volume down where nobody could accuse him of listening. “and nonna told the whole altar society you went to confession. she said it like *in california*. like it was fatima. mrs iannucci cried.”

The covers shift. “is the nun real.” “Go to sleep, Gina.” “that’s not a no.” It isn’t. Under the covers, at eleven at night, two thousand four hundred miles east, his sister waits for him to tell her what to do at eight in the morning.

choices.key: You gave Gina the nun’s advice: say his name.
response: “Say his name. Just ‘Danny.’ Then look at her till she looks away. Don’t explain and don’t defend. Make her hear it’s a person.” Silence under the covers while she turns it over. “who told you that.” “The nun.”
A much longer silence. Then, out loud, far too loud for eleven o’clock on a school night, loud enough that somewhere on Glenwood Avenue a bedroom door opens: “The nun is *real*?”

choices.text: “Say his name. Just ‘Danny.’ Then look at her.”
choices.key: You told Gina to say Danny’s name.
response: “that’s it?” “That’s it. Look at her till she looks away. Make her hear it’s a person.” Gina breathes in the dark awhile, deciding whether he’s an idiot. “ok.”

choices.text: “Ask her how her dad’s DUI is going.”
choices.key: You told Gina to ask Ashley about her father’s DUI.
response: “oh my *god*. jack.” He hears her sit straight up in bed. She is delighted. He can hear her composing it already, the timing, the face she’ll make, and he thinks of Ashley Vrabel in a color-guard jacket and his little sister with a rock in her hand. “Gina — ” “no. that’s good. that’s *really* good.”

choices.text: “He is in prison. So what. You get to be his sister anyway.”
choices.key: You told Gina she gets to be Danny’s sister anyway.
response: Nothing comes back for so long that he checks the bar. Then, small: “ok.” And smaller, from further under the blanket: “you sound like dad. when he had a job.”

choices.key: You told Gina to tell your mother.
response: “you’re such a narc.” “Tonight, Gina.” A sigh with all of Ursuline in it. Then, before she hangs up, so fast he nearly misses it: “fine.”

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Gina wants to know if the nun is real.

journal.text: Margot’s, by annexation: USEFUL IDIOTS FOR CHRISTIAN NATIONALISM, COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD. Sully’s made the board: liturgical football, idolatry, my outfit. Margot wasn’t even there when I read it. She didn’t need to be.

body: At 12:41 the Dell chimed on Jack’s desk with the only thing on the internet tonight that isn’t Patrick Swayze.

body.name: Becca Lindell ▸ Jack Costigan
body.text: BBQ + beach cleanup SATURDAY!! bring gloves :)

body: He owns gloves. Somewhere. Possibly in Ohio.

Swayze died yesterday — pancreatic cancer, fifty-seven — and the floor found out the way the floor finds out everything, laptop to laptop and door to door; at nine somebody down the hall had *Ghost* on with the volume up for the pottery wheel. Now it’s 2:52, and on Theo’s side of 412 it’s a different movie.

Theo is sitting up against the headboard in the Frette sheets with the MacBook on his knees and *Point Break* on the screen, sound low, no earbuds, because Jack is awake anyway and they both know it. Jack has been awake since a little after one. At 2:10 the freight came along the bluff and he counted it, and afterward he was still awake, on his back, listening across eleven feet of dark to Keanu Reeves learn to surf.
Theo knows every line and says none of them. Once, without looking over, he reaches across the gap between the beds and holds out the iPhone, screen first. It’s more than Theo has ever handed him.

body.text: i never saw it but im sad bc ur sad. is that dumb

body: “She’s fourteen,” Theo says. “I told her it was the least dumb thing anybody’s said to me this year and to go to sleep.” He takes the phone back. “She sent a frowny face and went to sleep. Fourteen is a wonderful age. Everything is either dumb or a frowny face.”

On the screen it’s the end of the world, or Australia: Bells Beach under a sky like wet slate, the fifty-year storm come in at last, waves standing up out of the sea like whole buildings making up their minds to fall. Swayze is soaked and bearded and older than he was an hour ago, and he wants to paddle out into it, and Keanu has hold of him.
“Everybody thinks the end is sad,” Theo says. His eyes don’t leave the screen. “Utah lets him go. That’s the nicest thing anybody does in the whole movie.”

choices.key: You told Theo that Lena knows about Danny.
response: Theo’s hand stops on the trackpad. “Good.” The screen. “Good for you, Costigan.” Then his thumb starts moving again, back and forth across the same inch of the trackpad, clicking nothing.

Utah unlocks the cuff. Swayze paddles out into the storm, and Utah throws his badge into the sea and walks back up the beach. The credits come up white on black. Theo shuts the MacBook on them and sets it on the floor, and for once 412 is properly dark: the standby light, the line under the door, nothing else.

Theo turns his head on the pillow and looks at him with real love. Then he does the rest of Pappas — the stakeout, the meatball sandwiches, the whole Busey jaw going at a sandwich in a parked car — perfectly, in a whisper, for a floor that isn’t asleep, and for a minute it’s just a dorm room at three in the morning, two guys and a movie.

Then Utah unlocks the cuff, and Swayze paddles out, and the badge goes into the sea. The credits come up white on black. Theo shuts the MacBook on them and sets it on the floor, and for once 412 is properly dark: the standby light, the line under the door, nothing else.

choices.text: Watch the end with him. Say nothing.
response: They watch it out. Utah unlocks the cuff. Swayze paddles out into the storm. Utah throws the badge into the sea, and across the room Theo’s breathing changes once, right there, and then goes back to what it was.
The credits come up white on black. Theo shuts the MacBook on them and sets it on the floor, and for once 412 is properly dark: the standby light, the line under the door, nothing else.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight.

s08.slug: TUESDAY · 3:40 PM · U.S. POST OFFICE, MISSION STREET
body: The flag out front is back at the top of the pole, snapping in the wind off the harbor as though Friday never happened.

La Flaca came down Mission on the rack on the front of the 11, and on the bus Jack counted the tip share in his lap, behind his backpack: singles, a five gone soft as cloth, quarters out of the jar by the register. He counted it twice. It came out the same both times.

There’s a line of four. A woman with a box taped at every seam as if it might try something. A man in a Raiders cap holding a passport application in both hands. A kid with a cello case who looks like he’s the one being mailed. Jack waits behind the cello.

The clerk has reading glasses on a cord and a Marisol Little League pin on her vest. “Money order,” he says. “Twenty dollars.” She keys it in. “Twenty-one ten.” He pays in singles and quarters, and she counts it again after him without comment, and the machine prints a United States Postal Service money order for $20.00.

He fills it out at the side counter with the pen on the bead chain. PAY TO: D. KOSTELNIK, in capitals. The address line he does without looking anything up, a street and a number his hand already knows, and then STRUTHERS, OH. On the line that says FROM he writes nothing at all.

The customer stub goes into his wallet, behind his Cardinal Mooney ID. The money order goes into an envelope, the envelope gets a stamp, and it goes through the brass slot marked OUT OF TOWN with a small flat sound, like a card laid face-down on a table.
He doesn’t think about it. He’s good at it.

Later La Flaca carries him down Mission to the wharf, to half-price chowder and the Hobart, and around ten the little TV over the Anchor’s counter shows the House voting to rebuke the congressman who yelled. Gloria turns it up. Rudy calls an order. Gloria turns it back down.

Lupe’s is where it always is, at the Las Olas end of Seacliff: a white truck under a string of chile lights and a line of people being honest with themselves at eleven at night. Two orders of carnitas and a horchata. The woman in the window says six dollars, and he has six dollars. After that the wallet folds flat around two IDs and a receipt.

On the door of 217 the whiteboard still says LANEY ♥ LENA and, under it, *ora pro nobis*. Inside, “You Belong with Me” on Laney’s iPod dock, on repeat, “in solidarity,” Laney says from the floor, “with a sister.” Jack knows the song personally. It was sung into the back of his neck by this same girl the whole way down Seacliff, his first night.

She’s on the carpet between the beds in her pref dress — white eyelet, a pageant habit, she has explained, because white photographs — with her legs straight out, her shoes under Lena’s desk, and her mascara cried off down to the freckles. Behind her on the bed Lena has a hairbrush and is taking the pins out of Laney’s hair one at a time and dropping them into a Café du Monde mug, each with its own small tick.

body.text: Lena looks up from the pins. “Mr. Costigan. You brought carnitas.” The address is still Monday’s. The look she gives the bag isn’t.
body.else: Lena looks up from the pins. “Costigan brought carnitas,” she tells Laney. “Say thank you.”

body: “I can’t eat,” Laney says. “I’m in mourning.” She eats. Pref Night, it emerges between bites, was the most beautiful thing that has ever happened to anybody — candles, the actives in a circle in white, a senior who cried so hard a contact came out — and Laney ruined it. “I *laughed*. A girl gets up and does a speech about her grandmother’s ring, very moving, and she holds it up, and y’all. It is a *mood ring*. It’s *purple*. And I laughed out loud in a room full of candles, and Sloane Kittredge looked at me like I’d brought a gun to a christening.”

She holds up the pink BlackBerry and plays a voicemail on speaker. A woman’s voice, bright as a stage: “Delaney Rose, it’s your mother. Posture, sweetheart. Posture. Call me after.” Laney lowers the phone. “Four-oh-two this afternoon. That’s the whole message. I’ve played it nine times. It doesn’t get any longer.”

Then the little silver pillbox comes out of her clutch, DRP on the lid, and she thumbs it open and takes one, dry, head back, the way you’d take a vitamin you’ve stopped believing in. “Doctor’s orders. I have a note.” Lena’s hands keep on with the pins. Jack watches her not say one word about it. The pins go on ticking into the mug.

By half past twelve the carnitas are gone and the horchata is gone, Taylor has started over more times than anybody has said out loud, and the mug is full. Laney’s hair is down, copper all over the white. She’s lying flat on the carpet now, looking at the ceiling, where somebody before them stuck glow-in-the-dark stars in the shape of no constellation at all.
“What if tomorrow,” she says, “they look at me, and they see.” She doesn’t say see what. On the bed, Lena’s brush stops.

response: Laney turns her head on the carpet. “You said that before.” “Still true.” She looks at him, and then back up at the stars, and lets him see her smile about it.

Later, when he shifts to get up, a hand comes out of all that white eyelet and takes his ankle. “Don’t leave. I’m not anything. But don’t.” He stays. By one she’s asleep on the carpet under Lena’s cardigan, and Jack and Lena sit against the two beds with the empty Lupe’s bag between them, whispering about nothing for five minutes — whether there’s a real Lupe (there is; gold tooth; Lena has met her), whether the Eagles know what’s coming Sunday. Then Lena pulls the cardigan up over Laney’s shoulder. “Cher,” she says, low, and reaches over and stops Taylor mid-chorus.

He gives her the full host: the invisible microphone, the teeth. “From Highland Park, Texas — five feet and one inch of copper and spite — her talent is the Jell-O shot, and her platform is *y’all* — ” Laney laughs, wet, the laugh you can hear across a party turned down to fit a dorm room, and points at him from the floor. “Shoulders, fireman. You’re hosting, not confessing.” He fixes his shoulders. She allows it.

Later, when he shifts to get up, a hand comes out of all that white eyelet and takes his ankle. “Don’t leave. I’m not anything. But don’t.” He stays. By one she’s asleep on the carpet under Lena’s cardigan, and Jack and Lena sit against the two beds with the empty Lupe’s bag between them, whispering about nothing for five minutes — whether there’s a real Lupe (there is; gold tooth; Lena has met her), whether the Eagles know what’s coming Sunday. Then Lena pulls the cardigan up over Laney’s shoulder. “Cher,” she says, low, and reaches over and stops Taylor mid-chorus.

Laney’s smile stays exactly where it is, and her eyes leave it. “Flying.” “You’re on the floor.” Over Laney’s head Lena looks at him — not angry; careful, like somebody watching a man wade out to where she knows the bottom drops. Laney rolls toward the bed and puts her face against the dust ruffle. “It’s a figure of speech, fireman.”

Later, when he shifts to get up, a hand comes out of all that white eyelet and takes his ankle. “Don’t leave. I’m not anything. But don’t.” He stays. By one she’s asleep on the carpet under Lena’s cardigan, and Jack and Lena sit against the two beds with the empty Lupe’s bag between them, whispering about nothing for five minutes — whether there’s a real Lupe (there is; gold tooth; Lena has met her), whether the Eagles know what’s coming Sunday. response: He sits down on the carpet with his back against Laney’s bed, and after a while, as if it had been settled somewhere, she shifts over and puts her head against his knee. Her hair smells of hairspray and Lupe’s. Lena goes back to the brush.

body: The eighth floor of the Brick is the silent floor, which means everybody on it whispers at the volume of normal conversation. A couple is breaking up by the photocopier in hisses. Somebody’s earbuds are leaking the new Muse. The windows look west at the Channel Islands, which are out there in the dark somewhere with no moon to find them by.

Kevin has a table by the glass: flashcards in four colors, rubber-banded by chapter, two Red Bulls sweating rings onto a napkin he brought for the purpose, and the maroon quarter-zip with BELLARMINE over the heart. He slides a can across. “Red Bull and shame. The shame’s mine. I got a B-plus on the first one.” He says *B-plus* like a diagnosis.

He warms up with dad jokes, as is his custom. “Why can’t you trust atoms?” “Kevin.” “They make up everything.” Jack puts his forehead on the table. “I had a chemistry joke,” Kevin says, “but all the good ones argon.” “It’s ten-twenty at night.” “That’s why I’m warming up. You don’t go into gen chem cold. That’s how people get hurt.”

Then the cards. Jack reads them out in a Youngstown accent that makes Avogadro sound like a guy with a body shop on Market Street, and Kevin answers every one before he’s finished. Somewhere around electron configurations, between chapters, Kevin talks about his summer: a Stanford program for pre-meds, and part of it was nights shadowing in a county ER in San Jose with a badge that said OBSERVER, so nobody would hand him anything sharp.

“Saturday nights are the worst,” he says, sunny, squaring a stack. “There was one in July. Two cars on Story Road. A minivan, a family, the dad driving, and a guy in a pickup who’d been at a barbecue since noon.” He snaps a rubber band around the stack. “They worked on the dad a long time. The little girl was okay. The guy in the pickup came in walking and sat in a chair in the hall and kept asking the nurses was he in trouble.” He looks out at the dark where the islands are. “The drunk one always walks out without a scratch. That’s how you know which one he is — he’s the one asking if he’s in trouble.”
Jack finds his own thumb on the scar through his eyebrow. Kevin, who is going to be a doctor, notices, and the smile comes back on. “What happened there, anyway?”

choices.text: A hockey puck. Youngstown Phantoms game.
response: “Hockey puck. Phantoms game, front row. They tell you to watch the puck, and I took it literally.” Kevin, clinically: “Pucks don’t cut like that. Pucks blunt.” “This one did. It was a playoff puck.” Kevin weighs it and decides to allow it.

At 11:58 the BlackBerry buzzes on the table, and the smile changes stations. Kevin answers in Vietnamese, fast and warm, and Jack catches nothing but the shape of it until the end: “Dạ, con đi ngủ rồi, Mẹ.” He hangs up and lays the phone face-down on the cards. “She thinks I’m asleep. She thinks a lot of things.” Then he cracks the second Red Bull.

choices.text: A Franciscan who plays dirty in pickup.
response: “There’s a Franciscan back home who plays pickup at the Y on Tuesdays. Brown habit, high-tops, rosary tucked in so it won’t swing. Elbows like original sin.” Kevin laughs — the real one, short and surprised, no team captain in it — and a girl two tables over shushes the whole eighth floor. “I’d believe that about a Franciscan.”

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Shadowed in an ER this summer. Tells his mother he’s asleep.

body.text: Two flights up from 217 at ten past one, the Lupe’s bag folded flat in his hand, the fourth-floor hall buzzing under its lights and La Flaca asleep against the radiator pipe.
body.else: In from the Brick at ten past one with Kevin’s flashcards still shuffling behind his eyes — Avogadro, Hund, the noble gases — the fourth-floor hall buzzing under its lights and La Flaca asleep against the radiator pipe.

body: 412 is empty, the lamp on. The RAZR, opened, shows one bar of battery, and then while he watches none, and then one again. His charger is plugged in behind the Hobart at the Anchor, where he left it Tuesday night and where it will still be at seven tonight.

Theo comes back from the showers down the hall in a towel, wet hair pushed back, his things in a leather case that has been to more countries than Jack has. “You have anything that fits a RAZR?” “Top shelf. The gray bag.” Theo points with his chin. “It’s in with the camera stuff. The Canon takes the same cable — mini-USB. It’s the only thing your phone and my camera have in common, Costigan. Treasure it.”

There are two bags on the top shelf of the closet. Jack goes up on his toes and pulls the one in front, the black one, because it’s in front: heavier than he expects, the zipper open halfway. He reaches in for a cable and comes out with denim.

A jacket. A women’s Levi’s jacket, small, the cuffs worn soft. He shakes it out to see what it is, and as it unfolds the back swings toward him, and on the back is Our Lady of Guadalupe, embroidered, a hand’s span tall: the blue-green mantle with its stars, the gold rays all around her, roses at her feet. Stitched by hand. He can see where the thread was knotted.
Theo crosses the room — it’s the fastest Jack has seen him move all week — and takes it out of his hands.

“A girl left it.” He’s already folding it, sleeves in, the back turned to the inside. “Brentwood girl. Marymount. She’s in Prague for the semester; she left it in the car, and I keep meaning to mail it to her. Nobody has an address in Prague. Have you ever tried to get an address in Prague? It’s all *ulice* this and *náměstí* that, and the post office is a palace, and the palace is closed.” The jacket goes into the black bag and the bag gets zipped, all the way, and Theo puts it back on the shelf himself, at the back. He takes down the gray one, finds the cable in a side pocket, and hands it over. “There. Mini-USB. A miracle of standardization.”
He gets into bed with the MacBook and his headphones on, and the menu screen of whatever it is lights his face blue and goes on looping, nothing playing.

choices.text: Say nothing. Plug in the phone.
response: Theo didn’t ask about the call from Trumbull, that morning in Malibu. Jack plugs the RAZR in at the desk, and the little light by the hinge comes on orange. Across the room the menu goes on looping on Theo’s face.
Theo keeps the headphones on. “It’s September,” he says. “Prague is lovely in September.” Jack plugs in the phone, and the little light by the hinge comes on orange.
“I’m going to.” Theo settles the headphones. After a while, on his side of the room, the movie starts.

body: Hollis 108 comes with its parade at ankle height — rainbow flip-flops, a skateboard, somebody’s golden retriever — and Evan Marsh is back. Last Thursday the door had a note on it. Today he’s on the front edge of the desk with the stained Carhartt over his chair and a bike clip still around the cuff of his jeans, grayer at the temples than Jack remembers, holding *Works of Love* in a library binding with the plastic jacket crackling.

body.text: Lena takes the desk two over from Jack’s, not the one beside it.
body.else: Lena takes the desk beside Jack’s.

body: Before Evan can open the book, Lena says it. “We read it. ‘Our Duty to Love the People We See.’ It was good.” Evan looks at her as if she’d spoken in a language he grew up in and hasn’t heard in years, and is trying to remember how you say *thank you*. Then he nods, and sets the book face-down on the desk.

They talk about Hale instead, because everyone does. This morning in Sandoval 1 Hale gave the four hundred the two drivers, slower and meaner than he gave them to the seminar, and finished on a line Jack wrote on the back flyleaf of the O’Connor: *The bill arrives at the wrong address. It always has.* The girl in the Marisol Surf hoodie wants to know if that means the one who hit the kid is worse or just, like, sadder. The Sigma Rho kid, visor backward, says it’s all luck, bro, you get pulled over or you don’t, and then hears himself and adds, “I mean morally.” Evan lets them go around twice.
Then, looking at the window rather than at any of them: “You’ve left out a driver. The one who stops, looks, sees nothing, and drives home.”

The room waits for the rest of it. Out the ankle-height window a pair of sandals goes by, and the shadow of a bike, and the clock over the door gets from 4:29 to 4:30 with a clunk. At 4:31 Evan picks the book back up. “Go love the people you see,” he says, and lets them out.

response: Evan is working the bike clip down over his other cuff. He keeps his eyes on it. “Section’s over, Mr. Costigan.” Not unkind. Just over.

response.text: Lena and Jack climb out into the four-thirty light. At the top of the steps she hitches up the tote and looks west, toward Seacliff and Bid Day. “Somebody has to be across the street, Mr. Costigan.”

journal.title: Evan Marsh (TA)
journal.text: Thursday section, Hollis 108. Kierkegaard. Kind to the scared ones, murder on the lazy ones. Smokes American Spirits. Rides a bike. Came back from PERSONAL grayer. Told us we’d left out a driver.
